t: The Celtic settlement of Medhelanon was taken by the Romans in 222 BCE; as Mediolanum it became an imperial seat under Maximian, and the Edict of Milan was issued from it in 313.

After the destruction of 1162 and a long struggle between the della Torre and the Visconti, the Visconti became dukes in 1395 and the Sforza took the city in 1450, before Spanish, Austrian and French rule.
The Five Days of 1848 and the defeat of the Austrians in 1859 brought Milan into the Kingdom of Italy, and in the 19th and 20th centuries it became the country’s industrial and financial centre.
dyk: Under the cathedral lie the ruins of the ancient church of Saint Tecla and the baptistery where Augustine of Hippo was baptised.
ev: A Celtic tribe of the Insubres settles Medhelanon
The Romans under the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus capture the settlement
Constantine issues the Edict of Milan from Mediolanum
Frederick I Barbarossa brings the destruction of much of the city
Francesco Sforza conquers Milan and ends the Ambrosian Republic
The Great Plague of Milan begins and kills an estimated 60,000 people by 1631
The Five Days rebellion forces Radetzky to withdraw temporarily
After the Battle of Solferino Milan and the rest of Lombardy are incorporated into Piedmont-Sardinia

f.founded: Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres group, of the Golasecca culture, settled it as Medhelanon; in the legend reported by Livy it was founded by Bellovesus in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus.
f.where: In the north-western part of the Po Valley in Lombardy, northern Italy, about halfway between the river Po and the foothills of the Alps, between the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east.
f.known: Mediolanum as an imperial seat; the Edict of Milan of 313; Bishop Ambrose; the Visconti and Sforza dukes; Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper; the Cathedral and the Castello Sforzesco; the Five Days of 1848
f.today: Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the second-largest city of Italy, with about 1.36 million people in the city proper.
